newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean oil firms' profits seen picking up in '97.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean oil firms' profits seen picking up in '97.

text.p: South Korean oil firms are likely to report sharply lower earnings for 1996, hit by huge foreign exchange losses, but prospects are rosier this year following price deregulation, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Oil refiners' profits should rise this year following deregulation in domestic oil product prices," said Bill Hunsaker, an energy analyst at ING-Barings Securities.
South Korea's move to open the energy sector was expected to put refiners on a more solid footing since it allowed them to raise prices, analysts said.
On January 1, the government freed price controls on domestic gasoline, kerosene, diesel and C-type fuel. Those products are no longer subject to a government-set monthly price ceiling.
Higher retail petrol prices would bolster refiners' profit margins and balance sheets, analysts said.
Despite recent falls in crude oil prices, refiners may be able to get away without cutting product prices, they said.
"As long as refiners don't start cutting prices to gain market share, profitability in the refining sector will improve," said Kim Sang-bae, an analyst at Ssangyong Investment Securities.
An increase in output of more value-added products after facilities were upgraded last year should also help company profits, he said.
Last year, refiners suffered heavily from the won's depreciation against the dollar despite reasonable operating profits, analysts said.
Foreign exchange losses accounted for 70 percent of total losses, they said.
"Foreign exchange losses should ease this year because the won is unlikely to decline as much as last year," Hunsaker said.
The won fell 8.2 percent against the dollar in 1996.
Yukong Ltd, the nation's largest oil refiner, is expected to post a net profit of about 65 billion won ($75 million) in 1996, down from 103.2 billion in 1995, a company official said.
The refiner saw 1996 sales at around 8.3 trillion won against 6.59 trillion in 1995.
"Decline in net profit is due mostly to foreign exchange loss," he said.
Ssangyong Oil Refining Co is forecast to record a net profit of about 120 billion won in 1996, little changed from 119.7 billion in 1995, a Ssangyong official said.
The firm estimated 1996 turnover at around 4.4 trillion won against 3.47 trillion in 1995.
Prospects for South Korean petrochemical firms, hit by high raw material costs and low petrochemical prices in 1996, continue to be bleak this year, analysts said.
"The price of naphtha, the feed stock, is likely to remain strong without much improvement in prices of petrochemicals," said Hunsaker.

Business was tough for petrochemical companies last year with analysts expecting Hanwha Chemical Corp to move into the red from a net profit of 50.6 billion in 1995 and LG Chemcial barely posting a gain of 3.3 billion against 91.2 billion a year earlier.
